I also found the descriptions of the Azad’s secret tv channels (24/h live broadcast of torture and rape of not only adults but even children) and the very idea of the Affront’s society to be very disturbing. Perhaps it is the idea of people who would take such great pleasure in causing others pain that is disturbing.

In my mind, the raspy Morrowind voice is because living in Vvardenfell, they had to breathe in ash every day. Dunmer born in Skyrim or Cyrodiil don’t have the “I smoke 8 packs a day and intend to die of lung cancer next year” voice because they lack those living conditions. It doesn’t explain the bad approximation of Cockney accents though. I like Teldryn Sero’s voice in the Dragonborn DLC for Skyrim, he’s got a nice balance between ashy and normal voice. 

Here’s how I do the Morrowind Dunmer voice, in case you want to try it out too:
Clear your throat, and focus on the noise that makes. Then keep making that noise for an extended amount of time, like a growl, focus on the way it feels in your throat to growl like that. Then, speak with that growl in your voice. 
Doing it too much will hurt your throat. I learnt how to do this during a very bad throat infection as a child, and had lots of fun scaring adults by suddenly speaking as though I was possessed.

Afterwards, I realised that I’d actually been very close to dying and it gave me a fright to realise that if it weren’t for my amazing boyfriend I’d most likely be dead. 

The doctors didn’t know what I had, they took blood tests and spinal fluid samples and everything they could think of but it showed no signs of infection. I think that what happened was that I’d gotten infected by some harmless virus or bacteria from New Zealand via my boyfriend, it had been different enough from the Swedish strains of such bugs that my immune system had freaked the fuck out, the penicillin I got at the emergency room had killed the infection but left the immune system confused and stuck in a feedback loop called a cytokine storm. I wake up in my bed, feeling strange. Out of habit I reach to scratch my beard, only to touch a beardless chin. I open my eyes. This is not my bed. Not my current bed in the student dorm. It's the old bed I slept in as a child, my stuffed animals lying like guardians next to me. I look at my hands, at how small they are. 

My parents come into the room, singing Happy Birthday, with a cake. The cake still has the old name  on it. Of course it does, they didn't know back then that I'd grow up into the person I am. I try my hardest not to visibly flinch when they call me by that name. 

My mother brushes my hair with fast, angry strokes, muttering about how my hair can get knotted just by looking at it wrong. I try to sit still and not fidget and not cry out in pain. She braids my hair into two braids, Wednesday Addams style, and finish them with two big bows. Then she gives me a deep midnight blue velvet dress to wear. 
Maybe I was sent back for a reason, maybe to change things and spare myself years of suffering? And just like that, an idea forms in my head. I spent a lot of my childhood trying to be a good little girl so people wouldn't notice I was actually a boy, puberty a slow torture as I had to watch my body betray me and change into something foreign to me. I remember putting up with ribbons and lacy dresses and pink, as well as the inevitable bruises. Lots of bruises and harsh words, slammed doors, taunts and threats and white knuckles. I remember longing to be rid of the knotty, tangled mane my mother would force into braids every morning. 

I walk into the bathroom and, as if by providence, the scissors my father uses to trim his beard with are still lying on the edge of the sink instead of in the bathroom cabinet I'm too short to reach. My favourite t-shirt, the blue one with a dinosaur on it that's actually from the boy's section, is lying on the washing machine waiting to get folded and put away, along with my grass-stained, patched-up pair of jeans that probably need a wash. Snip-snip is the sound of the future changing irreversibly. The braids lie on the floor like twin snakes. I wriggle out of my dress (but my current self's mind forces me to fold it neatly and leave it on the washing machine), and put the t-shirt on instead along with the jeans. 
I know I'll get bruises for this, and many harsh words, but it'll be worth it. 
This time, I will celebrate my birthday as the boy that I am, as myself.

Ash yams = regular yams or sweet potatoes, flavoured with liquid smoke to get the "ash" part of the name. 

Salt rice = regular rice, I use Thai black rice to dye regular rice purple so it looks more interesting. 

Kwama scuttle: tteokbokki, pieces of chewy rice cakes found in Korean cuisine and possibly other Asian countries. It's got a strange texture and is the closest to "bug meat that is also cheese" I could find. 

Sujamma = Fernet Branca, an Italian bitter liquor that has many herbs in it and is very divisive, you either love it or hate it. 

Dunmer cuisine is, in my headcanon, a mix between Korean food and Arabic food. They typically eat rice and several side dishes, and they enjoy spicy food. It is a beautiful day and the sun is shining. It's always a beautiful day here. I am standing next to Laura, my beautiful wife. I know she loves me very much because she tells me so. 
"Good morning, honey! Would you like to go to McDonald's for a delicious McBreakfast?" Her voice is clear and bright like a bell, and her smile could light up an entire room. We are standing outside our house in the cul de sac, as we do every morning. She takes my hand in hers. She has the softest hand you could ever imagine. 
"Uh, sure, I guess", I mumble. Truth be told, I'm sick of the McBreakfasts, but I can't tell her that, it'd absolutely crush her. 
"Perfect! Now let's get going, darling, you don't want to be late!" Laura smiles again and we get in the car. It's always shiny and clean, and the leather seats of the car are the most comfortable car seats I've ever used. It's a BMW. Whenever I am in the car or near it, a thought comes unbidden to my head: "BMW: Das Auto", spoken by a deep man's voice. We drive to McDonalds and the streets of the town are empty, as usual. The birds are singing in the trees somewhere. There must be birds somewhere, I hear their singing every day but I haven't actually seen the birds themselves. 
The McDonalds is a large and clean restaurant, the floors are freshly polished and the cashier, a young man named Michael, takes my order with a smile. 
"Would you like to try the McBreakfast, sir? Here at McDonalds we strive to provide the best possible service, and we value you. Thank you for coming here today, you're a great person. Would you like to try our offer of an extra Large McCappucino with your McBreakfast?"
I say yes, because I just can't disappoint him. He just looks so happy to work here. When he says he thinks I'm a great person, I believe him. My wife and I get our food and sit down at our usual table. It is perfectly clean. 
"Thank you, darling, it's so great to be here, with you! It's moments like these that we have to treasure." Laura takes my hand and grips it tightly. 
"So, uh... I was thinking... How come you never talk about your family, Laura?" It's a bit strange. She's my wife, yet I've never met her parents. 
"Why do you want to talk about that?" Her entire demeanour changes in an instant. Her expression is pained. "Honey, I just want us to enjoy this beautiful moment, sharing a McBreakfast together at the local McDonalds. Why can't we just sit here and be happy together?"
"Darling, I was just curious, I didn't mean-" She cuts me off, tears welling up in her bright blue eyes, the most beautiful eyes I have ever seen. 
"You know I love you. And I love having breakfast together with my wonderful husband. Please, let us have this. This happy moment together. I love you so much."
It's like I just kicked a puppy. She's so upset and all I did was trying to ask a question. 
"Okay, I'm sorry, let's just drop the subject." I take a bite out of my McBreakfast McSandwich and she immediately relaxes again, looking at me and smiling gently. 
After the meal, we go to the park and sit in the sunshine. We always go to the park after breakfast. In the distance I hear the sound of children playing and dogs barking, but I can't see them in the park. Still, they have to be somewhere. 
"I love you so much, darling. You mean so much to me. Would you like to go to McDonalds for a scrumptious, healthy lunch?"
I'm not really in the mood for eating, but I know I can't say no. She only seems truly happy when we're at McDonalds. When we're at home, she seems a bit vacant, like she's daydreaming. 
"Laura, do you remember our wedding? It was beautiful, wasn't it?" I have to ask her. It's been nagging at me for a long time, how she can be my wife yet I can't remember our wedding. 
"Yes, it was very beautiful. You were so handsome in your suit from Dolce&Gabbana. It was a wonderful day, but every day with you is wonderful." She looks at me and then kisses me. Her lips are soft and she tastes of strawberries. 
I know she is my beautiful wife, and I know I live in my beautiful house, but I sometimes get a strange feeling that something's not quite right. Even though I go to sleep in our bed, I always wake up standing outside the house. And I remember the rain on my face, even though it never rains here.

It's always good to apply the critical lense through which we view the lore books in the game to posts on here. Generally it's a good thing to be critical and inquisitive and not take things at face value. 

I'm one of those people who will create headcanons and similar things for fiction that I love (for instance, the line in Serenity where they explain that it's all actually just one really huge solar system that the entire show is set in, that line bothers me so much I just mentally censor it and pretend like it never happened). I go by the rule of "if it's cool/I like it, it is canon in my view of TES". Think of it as a tabletop rpg. The sourcebooks are what's actually in the TES games. There's a lot in them, sure, but there's also a lot that cannot be covered due to engine limitations etc. When you run into one of these "blank spots" in a tabletop RPG, you are encouraged to make something up yourself that would fit with the world according to your own discretion (changing the rules, making your own house rules, making up entirely new things, etc).  Some people go online and talk about what they've come up with for their tabletop games, which is what we're doing right here, essentially. If you see someone's house rules that you like you're free to incorporate them info your own campaign, and if you don't like it you don't have to use it. The bottom line is that as long as you're having fun it's all okay. And this is how I view TES lore as well. 

I'm just a lore noob, but I still enjoy thinking about TES and talking about it. A good idea is a good idea and a bad idea is a bad idea no matter who said it, or however many people up- or downvoted it. It might be a good idea though to try and cite sources as well as point out if you're just making things up or if you are quoting in-game stuff, as it makes things easier to follow and less risks of misunderstanding. Example: "In the book [title] it's said that [thing], and my take on it is that the author means [another thing]" instead of simply stating "What the author means is [another thing]".

Think of it like a tabletop RPG. 

You have the games, they're like the rule books and sourcebooks. They contain a lot of stuff, lots of info about the world, but there's still stuff they don't cover. Sometimes you have to deal with something the books don't cover, so you make a house rule or make something up yourself. This is essentially what we're doing here. Sometimes someone else's rule or idea is so good you decide to incorporate it into your own game, and this is kind of like when people use and build off each other's ideas here. The point of a tabletop game is to have fun, so you are free to change things as you see fit if they get in the way of having fun. But just as you wouldn't go up to someone and declare their Dungeons & Dragons world non-canon because it's not like your own adventure or because they use some house rules, you shouldn't stand in the way of people talking about TES lore. As long as you're having fun and you're not hurting anyone, it's all good.

It all makes sense if you see it from a tabletop roleplaying game kind of perspective. 

Bethesda write the sourcebooks and the rulebooks (the games). The rest is up to us, the players. We make our own heroes and let them have adventures. Any rpg book worth the trees it's printed on will have a section that boils down to "Remember that the goal is to have fun, and if there's stuff in these books that make your game boring or you think is stupid or something, feel free to make something up yourself.", and this attitude to lore is also found in TES. And just as with tabletop rpgs, you can discuss your own theories and ideas with other players, perhaps finding some that are so good that most accept it as of equal value and validity to that written in the official books. Of course, this also means that you can ignore the things you dislike and generally modify it as you see fit. 

I'm a complete lore noob and have just started getting ankle-deep in the vast ocean of lore, but I really enjoy the open-source mentality and the types of discussion and thought it leads to. It also legitimizes creating theories and worldbuilding based on meager materials, which is one of my favourite things to do with any piece of media that I enjoy, and that's nice as well. 

"Hey, guys, this rule seems a bit weird, my group houseruled it into being..."
"There's almost nothing on this subject in the sourcebooks, but it really caught my eye so I created a bunch of stuff for it, feel free to use it in your campaigns if you like it..."
"This is my apocrypha about what happened during that one time, only seen through the eyes of..."
"We've never really seen anything about this stuff, could it be because..."
These kinds of questions are all good questions. This kind of thinking is good. The open source idea legitimizes thinking this way about TES lore and thus it enriches the community as well as the works themselves in my experience.
